title: The ECB drains year-end liquidity while keeping its policy rate at 3%
summary: The ECB’s first press conference of 2000 combined a sizeable withdrawal of money-market liquidity with unchanged policy rates. The Governing Council kept the main refinancing rate at 3.0%, its marginal lending rate at 4.0% and its deposit rate at 2.0%. The separate €14.4 billion absorption on the morning of 5 January removed part of the exceptional liquidity made available against disruption around the century date change. Vice-President Christian Noyer explained that the operational aim was to let market rates trade around the existing 3% benchmark. President Willem Duisenberg’s inflation assessment, by contrast, concerned whether a temporary rise in energy, food and import prices might propagate into wages and other prices. Conflating the two decisions would turn an operational adjustment into a policy signal the speakers expressly disputed.

The risk premium associated with the date change had already fallen in late December and had disappeared by the market opening on 3 January. Financial intermediaries and payment systems had negotiated the transition smoothly. In the Q&A, a journalist compared the €14 billion actually drained, in rounded terms, with an intended €33 billion. Noyer explained that participants had offered less than the amount the Eurosystem considered consistent with an immediate return to normal conditions. Regular refinancing operations could complete the adjustment more gradually. The 3% ceiling on the fine-tuning operation was evidence of the intended benchmark. Duisenberg also rejected the suggestion that shifts in central-bank liquidity explained the recent run-up and reversal in global asset prices (opening remarks and Q&A on fine-tuning).

A separate monetary indicator pointed to ample liquidity at the broader economic level. The three-month average annual growth rate of M3 reached 6.0% in September–November, against 5.9% for August–October and a 4.5% reference value. Annual growth in loans to the private sector rose from 9.9% in October to 10.1% in November. These overlapping three-month averages and the individual monthly credit observations measure different quantities. Their joint relevance was that financing and monetary conditions remained generous even as one exceptional market operation was being unwound. Neither speaker treated a 1.5 percentage point overshoot of the M3 reference value as an instruction to raise the policy rate mechanically.

Economic activity reinforced the case for vigilance. The ECB reported improving global growth projections, US strength and a recovery in emerging Asia. A third-quarter euro area GDP estimate confirmed an expected upturn, industrial surveys pointed to solid output growth late in 1999, and continued employment gains and confidence supported the consumption outlook. Longer-term government bond yields had risen around 30 basis points since end-November. The opening statement attributed the rise partly to US yields and partly to improved prospects in Europe. This was a multiweek change preceding the event, not a measured response to the announcement. Duisenberg saw the potential for stronger relative European growth to support the euro, but gave no exchange-rate target or commitment to a change in exchange-rate policy.

The annual HICP rate rose from 1.4% in October to 1.6% in November 1999. Energy and unprocessed food accounted for much of the acceleration. Higher oil, earlier depreciation of the effective euro exchange rate and the fading effect of earlier food-price falls could push inflation higher in early 2000. The ECB envisaged a peak followed by moderation. Duisenberg cited a forecast of about 1.5% inflation on average for 2000 when questioned. A higher near-term reading was therefore consistent with the central projection. The material risk was that it might strengthen wage claims and set off a broader round of price increases. He gave no uniform numerical wage threshold and acknowledged that conditions differed across industries and regions, while expressing concern about settlements outpacing productivity.

A journalist asked whether the November rate increase had already dealt with this risk if inflation followed the expected path. Duisenberg declined to give the forward bias implicit in an affirmative answer. The combination of a hold, tighter operational liquidity and caution on wages consequently conveyed neither a pledge to keep rates unchanged nor a dated signal of renewed tightening. The immediate test for money markets was the restoration of normal trading around 3%; the test for expectations further along the curve was the composition and persistence of inflation after the anticipated early-year rise.

questions.question: Was the post-year-end move in money-market rates consistent with operational normalisation?
questions.detail: Noyer supplies a benchmark, an intended amount and the amount absorbed, but the transcript has no sequence of subsequent overnight fixings. Examine the Eurosystem’s dated fine-tuning and regular refinancing results alongside contemporaneous overnight and term quotes. Distinguish the known turn-of-year premium from revisions to expected policy. This bears directly on whether a short-end move warranted changing a view on the next Governing Council decision.

questions.question: Were wage settlements beginning to turn an imported price rise into domestic inflation?
questions.detail: Duisenberg identifies the channel but declines to quantify its probability. Compare wage agreements available at the time with sectoral productivity, and disaggregate subsequent price releases into energy, food and labour-intensive components. The comparison would help distinguish an anticipated increase in the price level from a persistent change in inflation dynamics relevant to medium-term rates.

questions.question: How much of the preceding long-yield rise reflected Europe rather than a global bond move?
questions.detail: The ECB gives two explanations for roughly 30 basis points of pre-meeting movement without allocating their shares. Compare contemporaneous US and European yield curves, rate futures and the timing of euro area growth news. That would help decide whether a position driven by European recovery primarily carried global duration exposure. The monthly figure alone cannot identify the announcement-day response.
